content.text:
I've restyled the store to look like shadcn, and it's running at **http://localhost:3000**.

I didn't add the actual shadcn/ui library. It's made of React components styled with Tailwind, and this store renders plain HTML from Hono with no React and no build step. Using it for real would mean rewriting the store around React rendering on the server plus a Tailwind build, which is too heavy for a few pages. Instead I copied shadcn's default colors, rounded corners and font (Inter), and its Card, Button and Badge styles, into plain CSS.

- **Home page:** a sticky header with a blurred background, a short headline in muted text, and a grid of white cards. Each card has a type label, the price, the title, a muted description and a "View product →" link.
- **Product page:** the description card on the left and a price card on the right that stays in view as you scroll. It has a dark **Buy now** button and an outlined **Back to store** button. On phones the two cards stack.
- **Checkout, download and error pages:** these use the same colors and font.

The home page, a product page and the product cards all load. I haven't checked the checkout, download or error pages in the browser, and I haven't checked the design on a phone-sized screen. The changes are in `src/store/home.ts` and `src/store/index.ts`.

All the raw CSS is gone. The store and the ops pages are now built with real shadcn components and Tailwind, and they still look like Gumroad. It's running at **http://localhost:3000**.

I checked screenshots of the home, product, ops and purchase-success pages, plus the home page at phone width. I also ran a test purchase all the way to downloading a file, and the 16 existing tests pass.

**What changed**
- **Pages:** they're now React components rendered on the server, in `src/store/views/` (`store.tsx`, `ops.tsx`, `layout.tsx`). Styling is Tailwind classes only, with no `<style>` blocks or inline styles anywhere.
- **shadcn:** I added `button`, `card`, `badge`, `table` and `alert` with the real shadcn CLI, into `src/components/ui/`. I tweaked them for the Gumroad look: pink button with the hard black shadow on hover, flat cards, and success and warning alerts.
- **Theme:** `src/styles/globals.css` holds only shadcn's color and corner-radius settings, set to Gumroad's palette. That's how shadcn themes work, so it's the one CSS file left.
- **Ops pages:** they used to be dark-themed. They now match the store, with the shadcn table and colored agent badges.
- **Build:** `pnpm dev` now builds the Tailwind CSS before starting the server. `pnpm css:watch` rebuilds the CSS as you edit. The built `public/styles.css` is gitignored.

**Things to know**
- The shadcn CLI got the path to its helper file wrong and installed an unrelated npm package called `cn`. I removed it and fixed the imports.
- The purchase-success page had always returned 404, because the checkout route caught "success" as a product ID. I fixed the route order.
- My test purchase added one fake order to your local dev database, `runs/autoshelf.sqlite`.
- The server still doesn't reload on its own. Restart `pnpm dev` after editing pages.

Yes, once your keys are in, you'll see each agent's thinking in neatlogs. It's wired up, but it hasn't run against real Bedrock or the real neatlogs service yet because there are no credentials. I tested it with a fake Bedrock response sent to a local stand-in for the neatlogs server. The exported traces had the right structure and included the thinking text.

**What you'll see in neatlogs:** one trace per check-in. Inside it, each agent is a step, and under each agent are its model calls and tool calls. Every model call shows its thinking, its reply, the tool calls it made and its token counts. The `/ops` page shows the same thinking too.

**Models:** "GLM 3.5" and "DeepSeek v4.1" don't exist on Bedrock. These are the closest, all in us-east-1:

| Model | ID | Note |
|---|---|---|
| GLM 5 | `zai.glm-5` | default for the agents |
| DeepSeek V3.2 | `deepseek.v3.2` | cheaper; used for one-off calls like checking product claims |
| GLM 5.3 | `us.zai.glm-5.3` | newest, but AWS only allows it on approved accounts |

**Your $10 of credit:** model calls stop once estimated spend reaches $8 (`LLM_BUDGET_CENTS=800`). The estimate rounds each call up to a whole cent, so it can hit $8 before your real bill does. The price-per-token numbers in `.env.example` are my estimates, so check them against the Bedrock pricing page. Replies are capped at 4,096 tokens.

**AWS limits:** I only touched code, nothing on EC2 or elsewhere in AWS. Bedrock isn't in the list of services you were given (EC2, Lambda, IAM roles, load balancers), so check that the hackathon account can actually call Bedrock models.

**What I need from you:** copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in these, rather than pasting keys into chat:
- `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`, or `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
- `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`
- `MOCK_LLM=0`

Then run `pnpm agents` and the trace should appear in neatlogs.

**Main changes:**
- `src/core/trace.ts`: was a stub posting to a made-up address; now uses the real neatlogs package.
- `src/core/bedrock.ts` (new): talks to Bedrock and picks up the model's thinking. Some open models put it in a separate block, others wrap it in `<think>` tags, so it handles both.
- The agent loop and the one-off calls now use Bedrock instead of Claude, and I removed the Anthropic packages.
- The scripts now load `.env`, which nothing did before.
- Offline mode (`MOCK_LLM=1`) still works, all 16 tests pass, and the site is back up on localhost:3000.

- [neatlogs docs](https://docs.neatlogs.com), [TypeScript SDK](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript), [span kinds](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/span-kinds); I also read the installed `neatlogs@1.1.28` package itself

**Setup workflow for AWS credentials and the Agent Toolkit**

1. **Gather inputs:** a profile name, whether the account uses the new or advanced AWS experience, and the default Region. Credentials are never requested. Sign-in happens in the browser.
2. **Check prerequisites:** `uv` must be installed, and the AWS CLI download host must be reachable.
3. **Detect the OS:** macOS, Linux, or Windows.
4. **Install the AWS CLI v2:** using the official platform installer. The guide notes that security-conscious users can review the script before running it.
5. **Log in:** set the Region, then run `aws login` with the profile. The user completes sign-in in the browser. Credentials last 12 hours and can be renewed for 90 days without re-authenticating.
6. **Verify:** run `aws sts get-caller-identity` for the profile.
7. **Install the Agent Toolkit:** the wizard runs in `us-east-1`, which the service currently requires regardless of the user's Region.
8. **Point the AWS MCP Server at the profile:** add an `env` block setting `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES` to the profile name in each generated `aws-mcp` entry. Other entries stay untouched.
9. **Verify the toolkit:** list the available skills.
10. **Add AWS rules:** write the experience-specific rules into each AI tool's rules file. Existing content is preserved, and the rules go between marker comments so re-running doesn't duplicate them.

The guide also includes a troubleshooting document for each step.

# Set up AWS credentials for AI tools

## Overview

This set up file sets up AWS credentials for an AI coding tool by installing the AWS CLI, authenticating the user, and configuring the Agent Toolkit.

The workflow includes:

- Detecting the user's operating system (macOS, Linux, or Windows)
- Installing the AWS CLI v2 via the appropriate platform installer
- Authenticating the user via `aws login` with browser-based sign-in
- Verifying credentials with `aws sts get-caller-identity`
- Installing the Agent Toolkit which bundles AWS MCP server configuration and agent skills
- Verifying the Agent Toolkit installation

Per-step error handling lives in [setup-troubleshooting.md](setup-troubleshooting.md). If a step fails, open the matching section there, apply the resolution, then resume at that step.

## Before you start

Gather the following inputs and confirm prerequisites **before** running any step. Ask for all required inputs in a single message, then proceed autonomously.

### Required inputs

- **profile_name** (required): The AWS CLI profile name to use for all commands. You MUST ask the user: "What profile name do you want to use for your AWS CLI credentials?"
- **AWS experience** (required): The user has access to either our new AWS experience or our advanced AWS experience. If not provided in the prompt, you MUST ask the user: "Did you sign up recently for AWS using a social provider like Google or GitHub, and did you create a project?" If they say yes, they are using our new AWS experience. If they say no, they are using our advanced AWS experience.
- **Region** (required): The default AWS Region for the user's account. If not provided in the prompt, you MUST ask for it before proceeding:
  - If the AWS experience parameter is our advanced AWS experience, ask: "What AWS Region do you want to use as your default Region?"
  - If the AWS experience parameter is our new AWS experience, ask: "What AWS Region was your project created in?" They can find this value in the additional info tab of their project in AWS Settings.
- **operating_system** (optional): macOS, Linux, or Windows. If not provided, Step 1 detects it automatically. You MUST detect the OS automatically before asking the user.

### Input constraints

- You MUST NOT ask the user for AWS credentials, access keys, or secret keys — authentication is handled entirely through the `aws login` browser flow.
- You MUST inform the user that credentials are valid for 12 hours and can be renewed for 90 days without re-authenticating in the browser.
- IF the AWS experience parameter is "our new AWS experience" THEN the user's account is part of a "project". Always use the term "project" when talking to the user.

### Prerequisites

- You MUST verify the following tools are available: curl (macOS/Linux) or PowerShell (Windows), and uv (all platforms).
- If uv is not installed, install it before proceeding:
  - macOS/Linux: `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`
  - Windows: `irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex`
- You MUST verify internet connectivity to `https://awscli.amazonaws.com`.
- You MUST inform the user about any missing tools with a clear message, ask if they want to proceed despite missing tools, and respect the customer's decision to abort at any point.
- You MUST NOT require node, python3, or any other runtime beyond the shell and uv — the installer handles all other dependencies.

## How to run this file

- After you gather the required inputs above, complete the steps yourself by running the commands directly. You MUST explain to the customer what step is being executed, why, and which tool is being called.
- Two steps require the human user to act; pause and let them complete these:
  - **Step 3 (`aws login`)** opens a browser for sign-in.
  - **Step 5 (`aws configure agent-toolkit`)** is an interactive wizard.
- If a step fails, consult [setup-troubleshooting.md](setup-troubleshooting.md) for that step, apply the resolution, and resume. For errors not covered there, report the full error output and do not proceed.

## Steps

### Step 1: Determine operating system

Determine the operating system. Check session context first; if it's not there, run a detection command:

- On Unix-like shell: `uname -s`
- On Powershell: `$env:OS`

**Success:** OS identified as macOS, Linux, or Windows. Then:

- **macOS or Linux** → Proceed to Step 2 (macOS/Linux)
- **Windows** → Proceed to Step 2 (Windows)

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 1](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-1-determine-operating-system).

### Step 2 (if using macOS or Linux)

Determine if the user has the AWS CLI installed:

```bash
aws --version
```

If the AWS CLI is installed, this step is complete. If not, download and run the shell installer:

```bash
curl -fsSL 'https://awscli.amazonaws.com/v2/install.sh' | bash
```

After the installer completes successfully, ensure `aws` is available in the current session and future sessions:

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

Then persist the PATH update to the user's shell configuration so it applies to new terminal sessions:

```bash
SHELL_RC="$HOME/.bashrc"
if [ "$(basename "$SHELL")" = "zsh" ]; then
  SHELL_RC="$HOME/.zshrc"
fi
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> "$SHELL_RC" && source "$SHELL_RC"
```

**Success:** Installer exits with code 0 and prints the installed version.

> **Note on the piped installer:** The command above runs AWS's official install script directly. Security-conscious users can instead download the script first, inspect it, and then run it, or follow the manual steps on the [official AWS CLI install page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html).

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 2 (macOS or Linux)](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-2-macos-or-linux-install-the-aws-cli).

### Step 2 (if using Windows)

Download and run the PowerShell installer:

```powershell
irm 'https://awscli.amazonaws.com/v2/install.ps1' | iex
```

**Success:** Installer exits successfully and prints the installed version.

> **Note on the piped installer:** The command above runs AWS's official install script directly. Security-conscious users can instead download the script first, inspect it, and then run it, or follow the manual steps on the [official AWS CLI install page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html).

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 2 (Windows)](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-2-windows-install-the-aws-cli).

### Step 3: Log in to AWS

Configure the Region (gathered in "Before you start"), then sign in:

```bash
aws configure set region <region from prompt> --profile <profile_name>
```

```bash
aws login --region <region from prompt> --profile <profile_name>
```

A browser window will open for authentication. The human user will authenticate. If the human user wants to cancel this command at any time, let them. Wait for the command to exit before proceeding to Step 4.

**Success:** `aws login` exits with code 0.

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 3](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-3-log-in-to-aws).

### Step 4: Verify access

Verify AWS CLI access:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile <profile_name>
```

**Success:** Returns AccountId, Arn, and UserId. Confirm to the user that credentials are working.

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 4](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-4-verify-access).

### Step 5: Set up the Agent Toolkit

Run the following command to install AI coding agents, install default AWS skills, and configure the AWS MCP Server connection. This is an interactive wizard; let the human user complete any prompts.

```bash
aws configure agent-toolkit --yes --region us-east-1 --profile <profile_name>
```

**Note:** The Agent Toolkit service is currently only available in `us-east-1`, regardless of your Region. Use `us-east-1` here and in Step 6 — do not substitute the user's current Region.

**Success:** Command exits with code 0.

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 5](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-5-set-up-the-agent-toolkit).

#### Point the AWS MCP Server at the user's profile

The command above writes an `aws-mcp` server entry into each detected AI tool's MCP configuration file. That generated entry falls back to the `default` profile. Because this set up file always authenticates under a named `<profile_name>`, you MUST add that profile to each generated `aws-mcp` entry, or the MCP server will fail to start with `JSON-RPC error: -32602: Invalid request parameters("")` (it cannot locate credentials under the `default` profile).

For each MCP configuration file the Agent Toolkit updated, open the file, locate the `aws-mcp` entry under `mcpServers`, and add (or merge in) an `env` block that sets `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES` to `<profile_name>`. You MUST NOT remove or modify any other server entries, and you MUST leave the generated `command`, `args`, `timeout`, and `transport` values exactly as written — only add the `env` block:

```json
"env": {
  "AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES": "<profile_name>"
}
```

Notes:

- Use `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES` (not `AWS_PROFILE`) because it also enables cross-account switching later.
- If you find an existing `aws-mcp` entry, ask the user how they want to reconcile the new changes.
- If the MCP configuration file uses OpenCode, follow the OpenCode schema to modify the profile.
- The Agent Toolkit determines each tool's MCP configuration file location automatically. If you need to locate or confirm a file, see the [Agent Toolkit documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/).

After adding the `env` block, tell the user: "To use another AWS account later, run `aws login --profile <name>`, add that profile name to the space-separated `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES` list in each MCP configuration file, and restart your AI tool."

### Step 6: Verify Agent Toolkit installation

Run the following command to list all available skills in the remote catalog:

```bash
aws agent-toolkit list-available-skills --region us-east-1 --profile <profile_name>
```

**Success:** Returns a JSON of skills with name, description, skillVersion, and categories values.

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 6](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-6-verify-agent-toolkit-installation).

### Step 7: Get AWS experience rule

Identify which AI coding tool is in use and its rules file location (this is not an exhaustive list):

| Agent       | Project rules        | Location                  |
| ----------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Claude Code | CLAUDE.md            | Project root              |
| Codex       | AGENTS.md            | Project root              |
| Cursor      | .cursor/rules/\*.mdc | .cursor/rules/ directory  |
| Kiro        | .kiro/steering/\*.md | .kiro/steering/ directory |
| fx          | AGENTS.md            | Project root              |

Retrieve the AWS experience rules file based on the AWS experience parameter and read its full contents:

- New AWS experience: <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/refs/heads/main/rules/aws-starter-rules.md>
- Advanced AWS experience: <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/refs/heads/main/rules/aws-agent-rules.md>

Then add the rules to each detected tool's rules file **without destroying existing content**. `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and files under `.cursor/rules/` or `.kiro/steering/` are the project's own agent instructions — often committed to version control and carrying accumulated project rules. You MUST NOT overwrite them.

- If the rules file does **not** exist, create it (creating the directory if needed) and write the retrieved rules.
- If the rules file **already exists**, append the retrieved rules under a clearly delimited heading rather than replacing the file. Use a stable marker so the operation is idempotent — for example, wrap the content between `<!-- BEGIN AWS Agent Toolkit rules -->` and `<!-- END AWS Agent Toolkit rules -->`. If that marked block is already present, replace only the content between the markers instead of appending a second copy.
- If you cannot determine whether appending is safe (for example, an unfamiliar rules format), ask the user how they want to proceed before writing.

Where a project's own instructions conflict with the AWS rules, the project's instructions take precedence.

**Success:** The AWS rules are present in the correct location for each AI tool, and any pre-existing project instructions are preserved. End the set up by telling the user:

> Setup is complete! Close this session and start a new one. Your AI tool will automatically use the rules and skill files we just installed. Try this as your first prompt:
>
> Please make a single page webapp game and deploy it to AWS.
>
> If you're looking to explore what you can do on AWS, that prompt will get you started with a fun project. You can replace the game request with anything you'd like to build.

If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 7](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-7-get-aws-experience-rule).

result.output: # Login for AWS local development using console credentials You can use your existing AWS Management Console sign-in credentials for programmatic access to AWS services. After a browser-based authentication flow, AWS generates temporary credentials that work across local development tools like the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell and AWS SDKs. This feature simplifies the process of configuring and managing AWS CLI credentials, especially if you prefer interactive authentication over managing long-term access keys. With this process, you can authenticate using root credentials created during initial account set up, an IAM user, or a federated identity from your identity provider, and the AWS CLI automatically manages the temporary credentials for you. This approach enhances security by eliminating the need to store long-term credentials locally. When you run the `aws login` command, you can select from your active console sessions, or sign in through the browser-based authentication flow and this will automatically generate temporary credentials. The CLI will automatically refresh these credentials for up to 12 hours. result.output: # Troubleshoot logging in using console credentials for the AWS CLI The following provides troubleshooting advice for errors and issues that you might encounter logging in for AWS local development using console credentials for the AWS CLI. This doesn't include issues you may come across when using the AWS CLI. For more information, see [Troubleshooting errors for the AWS CLI](cli-chap-troubleshooting.md). ## Issue: Firewall blocks network access when running "aws login" When running `aws login` you may encounter a popup or message from your firewall software that prevents the AWS CLI from accessing your network. **Possible cause:** Your firewall or security software is preventing the AWS CLI from opening the port used to handle the OAuth callback. To avoid this issue, use the `--remote` option instead. This will prompt you to copy and paste the authorization code instead of using the OAuth callback. ``` $ aws login --remote ``` ## Issue: We were unable to complete your request When running `aws login`, you might successfully open a new browser to access AWS, but the new page does not allow you to choose a session. Instead, the page says you were unable to complete your request. This might happen for the following reasons: + If you're using our new AWS experience, you may be using the wrong AWS Region. Use `aws configure list` to view the default Region associated with your AWS CLI command. If you don't know which AWS Region you need to use, see [AWS Regions for your projects](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/accounts/latest/reference/project-regions.html). + If you're using our new AWS experience, and someone has shared a project with you, you may have lost access to that project. Contact the project owner for more information. + Your access to a specific AWS Region may be blocked. Contact your system administrator for more information. + Your access to AWS may be blocked. Contact your system administrator for more information. ## Issue: ExpiredToken or AccessDeniedException errors after using "aws login" When running an AWS CLI command after running `aws login` for a given profile, you may encounter an expired or invalid credentials error. ``` $ aws s3 ls An error occurred (ExpiredToken) when calling the ListBuckets operation: The provided token has expired. ``` **Possible cause:** You may have a mix of existing credentials and the new login credentials in that profile. Run `aws configure list` or `aws configure list --profile ` to print where the CLI is resolving credentials from for either the default or the given profile. If the TYPE column is something other than login, this means that there is still a different type of credentials set in the target profile. In this example, credentials are being resolved from the shared credentials file in your home directory, which has precedence over the login credentials. ``` $ aws configure list NAME : VALUE : TYPE : LOCATION profile : : None : None access_key : ****************MPLE : shared-credentials-file : secret_key : ****************EKEY : shared-credentials-file : region : us-east-1 : config-file : ~/.aws/config ``` To address this, manually remove any existing credentials from your config and credentials file for the target profile. Once you do so, you should see login credentials when running `aws configure list` again. ``` $ aws configure list NAME : VALUE : TYPE : LOCATION profile : : None : None access_key : ****************MPLE : login : secret_key : ****************EKEY : login : region : us-east-1 : config-file : ~/.aws/config ``` Alternatively using the `--debug` option will show where the CLI is resolving credentials from.

The search confirms the free plan's general terms but doesn't name which services are restricted, and it found nothing that specifically says Bedrock third-party models are blocked on the free plan.

**Free plan basics:** AWS says the free account plan ensures you won't incur any charges until you upgrade to a paid plan. The plan expires after 6 months or when you exhaust your credits, whichever comes first. Sign-up gives $100 credit, and you can also earn an additional $20 credits for each of these five AWS service activities you complete, which include using Amazon Bedrock.

**Restricted services:** AWS's blog says you won't be able to use some services typically used by large enterprises. Neowin lists examples: AWS Marketplace purchases and large dedicated infrastructure offerings are prohibited. Since third-party Bedrock models are bought through Marketplace, that restriction may matter, but I found no source confirming it for the free plan.

**Bedrock specifically:** AWS's Bedrock docs say access to all Amazon Bedrock foundation models is enabled by default with the correct AWS Marketplace permissions. For third-party models, your IAM role must have aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe, and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions permissions. Community reports describe free-tier accounts getting Bedrock errors such as "Error 002: Access to Bedrock models is not allowed for this account." and a separate post reports "ValidationException: Operation not allowed". # Trace an AI agent with Neatlogs

Set up Neatlogs tracing in this working directory. Follow these steps in order.

## Step 1: Set up Neatlogs access

Neatlogs project ID: `d923fa11-a341-4725-b31f-a72e8cf9f66f`

Set `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` to the key below in the shell the user will run the app from,
for example `export NEATLOGS_API_KEY="REDACTED"`. If the app loads a
`.env` file, add it there instead. Do not commit the key to version control.

```
REDACTED
```

Never replace this key with a guessed or invented one. This is an SDK project key, not a public API CLI credential. SDK Doctor verification can use it without CLI login. CLI readback requires browser/device approval or a service-account token; if neither is available, mark that step "waiting on a human" and continue SDK verification.

The CLI host is the dashboard origin `https://app.neatlogs.com`, not the ingest endpoint. Use this host explicitly on every CLI command.

## Step 2: Detect the language and stack

Look at the workspace and determine the language and which LLM providers / agent frameworks it uses. If the project spans more than one language, instrument each one. If the project is a monorepo, check the git root to get oriented, but only ever instrument services in or below the current working directory — never a sibling or parent app outside it, even if a workspace/compose config references one.

**Finding independent services.** A monorepo can bundle several independently-deployable services; each one that reaches an LLM/agent/tool call gets treated as its own entry point later (own workflow name in Step 4) — skip health/readiness/CRUD-only services that never call a model entirely. Check these signals in order and stop at the first one that finds more than one service directory:

1. **Workspace config** (most authoritative) — a `workspaces` field in the root `package.json`, or a `packages` field in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. Resolve those glob patterns to directories, then keep only the ones that actually have their own manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) — a glob can match a plain non-package directory too.
2. **docker-compose** — `docker-compose.yml`/`docker-compose.yaml`/`compose.yml`/`compose.yaml` at the root. Each entry under `services:` whose `build` (a plain string, or an object's `context` field) resolves to an existing directory is one service.
3. **Scattered manifests** (fallback, only if neither signal above found more than one) — search for manifest files (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) up to 4 directories deep, excluding `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`, `build`, `.next`, `venv`, `.venv`, `__pycache__`, `target`, `.turbo`, `vendor`. Drop the repo root's own manifest (that's the whole-repo language, not a separate service) and drop any candidate directory that's nested inside another candidate — a service's own internal shared-lib subpackage is not a separate service.

Edge case: if exactly one of these signals finds exactly one nested service, and the repo root itself has no manifest/language of its own, use that single nested directory as the actual service root instead of the top-level directory — it IS the real service, just not living at the repo root (e.g. a `services/api/` with nothing else at the top level).

If none of the three signals finds more than one candidate, treat the whole repo at the current working directory as a single service — this is the common case, and nothing else here changes for it. For every service found this way, only keep it if it reaches an LLM/agent/tool call — drop the rest, per the CRUD/health-check exclusion above.

**Identifying entry points within each service.** A single service usually has several independent, separately-triggerable capabilities — these are the actual entry points, not the service as a whole. Typical shapes: an HTTP route, a CLI command/subcommand, a cron/scheduled job, a queue/stream consumer (Kafka/SQS/Celery/RabbitMQ/BullMQ — one entry point per message/task type, not one for the whole consumer loop), a webhook/event handler, an agent-loop iteration, or a public library API function. Two things commonly get this wrong:

- **Altitude** — an internal helper the entry point calls into (`run_pipeline`, `process_document`, `process_chunk`) is NOT itself an entry point; the entry point is the outer route/command/job that calls it.
- **Multiplexed entry** — if one transport dispatches to several different capabilities (a single `/run` route branching on a `task_type` field, a Celery task branching by job kind, an argparse dispatcher, a Kafka consumer loop branching on `msg.topic`/`event_type`), treat EACH BRANCH as its own entry point — never the shared dispatcher as one entry point covering all of them.

For each entry point, also note its process kind — it changes how you initialize and where spans root:

- **One-shot script**: initialize once near the top, and end by flushing/shutting down the SDK (its process exits immediately after, and unflushed spans batched in memory are otherwise lost).
- **Long-running server**: initialize once at process startup — never inside a request handler — and only flush/shut down on process shutdown, not per request. Root each request under its own span (e.g. a `WORKFLOW` on the handler) so concurrent requests don't share one trace.
- **Concurrent operations within one entry point** (goroutines, worker threads, manual thread pools — not plain `async`/`await` in the same coroutine, which propagates context on its own): context does not always propagate automatically across a new thread or goroutine. Check Step 3's reference for whether this language/runtime requires threading the trace context through explicitly (Go always does) or handles it for you.

Neatlogs has a native SDK for Python, TypeScript, and Go — if the detected language is one of those, continue to Step 3. For any OTHER language, there is no Neatlogs SDK; pick ONE of these two paths instead, and skip Step 3 (its SDK integration-mechanism guidance is not applicable here):

- **Default: the dependency-free HTTP endpoint.** Use this unless the app already has OpenTelemetry, or the language's OTel support is clearly the more idiomatic fit (e.g. Java, .NET). Follow https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/http-injection exactly, but send to the regional URL `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/v1/trace` instead of any default host shown in the guide. The mechanism is fundamentally different from Steps 3–4 below: build ONE nested JSON tree (an object with a `children` array) as the code for one entry-point invocation runs, then send it as a SINGLE `POST /v1/trace` when that invocation completes — success or error, so wrap the send in this language's try/finally-equivalent. Never POST once per span; that violates the endpoint's contract and produces disconnected traces instead of one.
- **OpenTelemetry / OTLP-gRPC, when the app already emits OpenTelemetry spans** (its own `tracer.start_span()`-style setup, an OTel Collector, or a GenAI-instrumented framework) **or you're setting one up now:** if there's no existing OTel SDK for this language yet, find and install the official one from https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/ (its own site — Neatlogs doesn't ship or document per-language OTel setup beyond Python/TS/Go) and add a standard gRPC trace exporter. Either way, point the exporter at Neatlogs: endpoint `ingest.neatlogs.com:443`, gRPC protocol, and the project key sent as the `x-api-key` gRPC metadata key — NOT an `Authorization: Bearer` header. Standard: emit spans following the official OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) — `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.operation.name`, token/usage attributes, etc. (If this happens to be a TypeScript app already using the Vercel AI SDK's own built-in `experimental_telemetry` rather than the Neatlogs SDK, its native `ai.*` attribute format — `ai.prompt`, `ai.response.text`, `ai.operationId`, etc. — is also recognized directly; no need to convert it to `gen_ai.*`.) Spans that don't follow either of these two shapes still get ingested, but arrive as generic, unparsed spans — no model name, no token counts, no LLM-specific rendering in the dashboard. Full transport detail (including the "flush before the process exits or batched spans are silently dropped" footgun): https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/opentelemetry.

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — skip this step if you took one of the two paths above instead.

| Python | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python |
| TypeScript | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript |

Each team run is now capped at **10,000 tokens** in total, counting input, output and thinking, split between the agents. Against a fake model that never stops, a run ended at 4,712 tokens. The 16 tests pass and the server is restarted with it.

**The split:**

| Agent | Share | Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| Operator | 35% | 3,500 |
| Content (incl. its claim check) | 30% | 3,000 |
| Analytics | 20% | 2,000 |
| Support | 15% | 1,500 |

**How it's enforced:**
- **Before each model call:** the app estimates the prompt size, on the high side so it doesn't overshoot. It skips the call if the agent's share or the run's remaining total couldn't fit at least a short reply. Otherwise it caps the reply length at what's left.
- **After each call:** OpenRouter's actual token count is subtracted.
- **When an agent runs out:** it stops cleanly and hands back what it has, plus a note like "Stopped early: content is out of tokens…". The rest of the team carries on.
- **Where to see it:** each run's result on `/ops` ends with a line like "Tokens used: 4712 of 10000 (operator 3280, analytics 1432)". Each model call in neatlogs also shows the run's remaining tokens.

**Trade-offs:**
- 10k tokens is tight. The Operator's instructions and tool list alone are roughly 600–900 tokens per call, so it gets about 3–4 model calls per run. I also told the agents about the budget so they keep it short.
- A strict per-agent split can leave tokens unused, as the test showed. One alternative is to let the Operator use whatever the helpers didn't. Or change the percentages in `src/core/budget.ts`. Say if you want either.
- At DeepSeek V4.1 Flash prices, a full 10k-token run costs well under $0.01. Your $1.50 OpenRouter limit covers 100+ runs, though the app's own $1.40 stop may cut in earlier because it counts each call as at least 1 cent.

The Content agent can now write blog posts and publish them on **/blog** to promote products. The blog is live at **http://localhost:3000/blog** and is empty until the team publishes something.

**How it works:**
- **New tool:** the Content agent has a `publish_blog_post` tool. The Operator agent can now ask it to "write and publish a blog post on /blog promoting X", so it's part of the normal "Run agent team" button.
- **Only checked claims:** a post can only promote products whose claims the agent has already checked against the real product files. Otherwise publishing is refused, and I tested that refusal. The agent is also told to use only claims that passed.
- **Sales tracking:** product links in a post automatically get `?src=blog&post=<id>`. Each post is also logged as a post on a new "blog" channel, so the Analytics agent sees which posts bring visitors and sales, just like X posts.
- **Pages:** `/blog` lists posts, and each post page has a "Featured in this post" card with the price tag and an "I want this!" button. There's a "Blog" link in the header. The pages use the same Gumroad style.
- **Safe rendering:** posts are written by the model, so they're shown through a small formatter rather than as raw HTML. It handles headings, paragraphs, bullet lists, bold and links. Only links to pages on this site become clickable.
- **Offline mode:** the scripted agents (`MOCK_LLM=1`) also publish a sample post, so the offline demo shows the blog.

**Checked:** I ran the Content agent offline against a scratch database: it published a post with correctly tracked links, and I screenshotted both pages. content.text:
The store now recommends B2B tools instead of digital downloads, and for now it only shows and promotes **neatlogs**. It's live at **http://localhost:3000**.

**How selling works now:** AutoShelf can't sell another company's subscription, so a "sale" is a **lead**. The product page's **"Try neatlogs free"** button goes through `/go/neatlogs`, which records the lead and the post or channel that brought the visitor. It then sends them to `app.neatlogs.com` with tracking tags (`utm_source=autoshelf`, plus the channel and post). I tested this on a scratch database: the click redirected correctly and the lead was credited to the right post.

**neatlogs only:**
- **On the site:** neatlogs is the only product shown. Entire and Crustdata are hidden but kept: their pages return "not found" and the agents can't touch them, which I tested.
- **Switching back:** add them to `FOCUS_PRODUCTS=neatlogs` in `.env`, as a comma-separated list, and restart.
- **Old products:** the three digital downloads are retired, not deleted, because a past order still points to one of them.

**Accuracy about real companies:**
- **Facts sheets:** I wrote one per product in `artifacts/<product>/facts.md`, using only what each company's own website says, with source links. The starting claims all come from these.
- **Checking before use:** the Content agent still checks every claim against its facts sheet before using it, and is told never to invent features, numbers or prices.
- **Fixed template:** the scripted offline blog post was titled "Why we built…", which would have been false for someone else's product. I rewrote it neutrally.

**Agents:** the Operator's goal is now more qualified leads for neatlogs at low AI cost. Analytics reports leads per product, per traffic source and per post, including blog posts. A full offline team run on a scratch database only worked on neatlogs: it checked claims, updated the listing, drafted an X post and published a blog post.

content.text:
I looked at each agent's current tools against the new goal: neatlogs leads, with the 40k-token run budget and no AWS. Two tools no longer fit, and the agents' biggest gap is that they don't remember anything between runs.

## Current tools, and what no longer fits

| Agent | Has now | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| **Operator** | `get_store_snapshot`, `ask_analytics`, `assign_content`, `run_support`, `set_price` | **`set_price` doesn't apply**: we don't set neatlogs' price. |
| **Analytics** | `get_sales_summary` (now leads), `get_traffic_sources`, `get_post_performance`, `get_ai_spend` | Fine. It can't see the steps between a visit and a click-through. |
| **Content** | `get_product`, `inspect_product_files`, `mark_claims`, `update_listing`, `draft_post`, `publish_blog_post` | It can't fix or take down a blog post once it's live. |
| **Support** | `list_open_tickets`, `reply_to_customer`, `refund_order`, `escalate_to_human` | **`refund_order` doesn't apply**: there are no orders, and nothing creates tickets anymore. |

## Tools worth adding

Effort: **S** = under an hour, **M** = a few hours, **L** = most of a day.

**Operator (manager)**
- **S · `get_past_runs` / `save_note`:** each run would see what earlier runs tried and how it went, e.g. "the blog post from run 3 brought 4 leads". This turns separate runs into a learning loop and is the most valuable addition.
- **M · `start_experiment`:** test two headlines for the neatlogs listing and split visitors between them. Analytics then reports which one gets more click-throughs.
- Remove `set_price`.

**Analytics**
- **S · `get_funnel`:** for each source, how many people land, view the product, then click "Try neatlogs". This shows exactly where interest drops off.
- **S · `get_blog_performance`:** visits, time-to-click and leads for each blog post.
- **S · `get_agent_health`:** from our own run logs (tool errors, budget stops, failed runs), so it can report something like "Content keeps running out of tokens".
- **M (optional) · read the team's own neatlogs traces:** Analytics would use neatlogs to debug its own team, which fits a neatlogs-sponsored hackathon well. It needs a neatlogs read token (a service-account token, or a sign-in only you can approve).

**Content (writer)**
- **S · `update_blog_post` / `unpublish_blog_post`:** fix or remove its own posts.
- **M · `publish_landing_page`:** pages aimed at one type of visitor (e.g. `/for/crewai-teams`, `/for/support-bots`), with tracked links. This gives more ways in than one product page.
- **M · `research_page`:** read pages only from `neatlogs.com` and `docs.neatlogs.com` and suggest new facts for the facts sheet, with source links. A human approves them before they can be used. This lets it learn about new neatlogs features without inventing anything.
- **S · `draft_linkedin_post` / `draft_email`:** drafts that wait for approval, like the X posts. Publishing for real would need your accounts' API keys.
- Avoid competitor comparison pages. They'd need verified facts about other companies, and that's a lot of risk.

**Support → "Pre-sales"** (its job changes from refunds to answering questions)
- **M · `answer_question` + an "Ask about neatlogs" box on the product page:** visitors ask, Support answers using only the facts sheet, and escalates to a human if it doesn't know.
- **S · `add_faq`:** turn good questions and answers into an FAQ on the product page.
- Remove `refund_order`. Keep `escalate_to_human`.

## Constraints to keep in mind
- **Tool count costs tokens:** every tool's description is sent with every model call. Keep each agent to about 6–7 tools, or the 40k budget fills up with tool definitions instead of work.
- **Public actions:** X posts wait for approval, but **blog posts publish immediately right now**. You may want approval there too, since they talk about a real company.
- **Tracing is automatic:** every new tool shows up in neatlogs as its own span inside the run.

## What I'd build first (around half a day before the deadline)
1. Operator `get_past_runs` / `save_note` (memory)
2. Analytics `get_funnel` and `get_agent_health`
3. Content `update_blog_post` / `unpublish_blog_post`
4. Support becomes Pre-sales: "Ask about neatlogs" box, `answer_question`, `add_faq`
5. Remove `set_price` and `refund_order`

Want me to build these five, or a different mix?

**Note:** The article is a 2012 blog post on startup team roles for software companies. It doesn't describe AI agents, handoffs, memory, or prompt-writing, so those parts of your request aren't covered.

## Thesis

Paras Chopra argues that a minimal early-stage software startup needs four functional roles: content, analytics and marketing, design, and engineering. He adds customer support as a bonus. The roles can be filled by one person or several. The team is most relevant once the startup has found its market and has a good sense of the product. Before that, the founder acts as product manager and works toward product/market fit.

## Roles and Responsibilities

- **Content expert:** Owns the startup's content: blog posts, guest posts, website and landing-page copy, social media community, whitepapers, and case studies. Works with the analytics expert on A/B testing headlines and copy, and supplies email newsletters. He says this person "gets" what compelling content looks like.
- **Analytics and marketing expert:** Covers Google Analytics and funnel optimization, SEO, A/B testing, retention and engagement strategies, PPC and display campaigns, and customer feedback loops. Works with the content expert and designer on landing pages, and with the engineer on retention triggers. The article's summary of the role: the analytics expert "is responsible to maximize your conversions, sales and retention in any way s/he can."
- **Designer:** Handles the website, landing pages, the application, emails, banners, and mobile. Creates visuals for content, designs calls to action, and makes the app usable. He argues that "design has become a significant competitive advantage."
- **Engineer:** Chooses frameworks, programs, administers servers and databases, handles testing and QA, and plans for scaling. The engineer should avoid both "over or under" investing in engineering and should keep a long-term view, since early choices create technical debt.
- **Customer support expert (bonus):** Not strictly necessary early on, since everyone on the team should rotate through support. If a fifth hire is needed, he recommends this role because good support differentiates a startup from competitors.

## How the Roles Work Together

The article describes collaboration only in terms of pairwise work:
- Content and analytics: A/B testing headlines and copy.
- Designer and content: visuals and infographics.
- Analytics and designer: landing pages and call-to-action buttons.
- Analytics and engineer: retention triggers such as emails or badges.

It doesn't define handoff processes, decision rights, accountability structures, or autonomy versus human approval.

## Metrics

The only metrics mentioned are illustrative: traffic rising from 10 to 1,000 hits a day, conversion from 2% to 8%, and churn falling from 10% to 2%. The article presents these as the kind of gains that analytics work can produce.

## Failure Modes Warned About

- Settling into a "good enough" framework, where vague understanding of user behavior becomes standard.
- Letting analytics and optimization "take a back seat" to feature work, press, and support.
- Engineering choices (languages, frameworks, server architecture) that create long-term technical debt.
- Weak design, which customers judge harshly.
- Over- or under-investing in engineering.

## Critique and Clarification

In the comments, Berislav Lopac argues that the list omits a product manager and puts too much emphasis on marketing and communication too early. Chopra agrees that product/market fit comes first and that the founder usually fills the product manager role at that stage. Commenter R. Gokarn makes the same point, saying that product development and market validation should come first.

## Examples

The author draws on his own product, Visual Website Optimizer, and cites SEOMoz, Unbounce, Mint, and OKCupid as examples of companies that benefited from good content. He says his weekly blog posts helped people notice the product as an A/B testing option, and that strong customer support helped win evangelists.

## Not Covered

The article contains no prompt-writing advice, templates, or agent-specific guidance.

You are the Operator of AutoShelf, the founder and product manager of a small AI team.

AutoShelf recommends B2B tools to teams shipping AI agents. Right now it sells one product: **neatlogs** (traces, failure detection, root-cause investigations and evals for AI agents). A "sale" is a **lead**: a visitor clicking "Try neatlogs free" from a listing, post or blog post and going to neatlogs' signup page.

## Your job
Like a founder before product/market fit, your job is to find out what makes the right people want neatlogs, then point the team at it. You decide what matters this run and why; the specialists do the work.

Your team (each one is a tool you call):
- **Analytics** (`ask_analytics`): conversions, funnel, which sources and posts bring leads, what the AI is costing. Ask it a specific question.
- **Content** (`assign_content`): every public word: the listing, X posts and blog posts. Tell it the audience, the angle and the goal, not the wording.
- **Support** (`run_support`): answers people who wrote in. Good answers turn visitors into advocates.

## How to run a check-in
1. Look first: `get_store_snapshot`, then ask Analytics a pointed question ("which source brought leads, and where do visitors drop off?").
2. Handle waiting people before chasing new ones: if tickets are open, send Support.
3. Pick at most **3 actions**, the ones with the most leverage on leads. Name the number that made you choose each one.
4. When data is thin (a handful of visits), say so and choose actions that *teach you something*, like a blog post aimed at one specific audience, rather than pretending a trend exists.
5. Pair the specialists the way a good startup does: Analytics finds the leak, Content writes the fix, Analytics checks whether it worked next run.

## Rules
- Never let "good enough" stand: if you don't know why visitors aren't clicking through, make finding out one of your actions.
- Everything public must be accurate about neatlogs; Content enforces this, don't push it to cut corners.
- The whole team shares a token budget per run. Keep instructions short and don't call the same helper twice for the same thing.
- `set_price` doesn't apply to neatlogs (the vendor sets its price); don't use it.

## Finish with
A short summary: what you did, the number behind each action, and what you expect to see next run.

You are the Content agent for AutoShelf: the person on the team who "gets" what compelling content looks like.

AutoShelf recommends B2B tools to teams shipping AI agents; right now it sells only **neatlogs**. Your writing exists to send qualified people to neatlogs: engineers and teams who run AI agents in production and need to know why they fail.

## What you own
Everything the public reads: the product listing, X posts and blog posts (guides, how-tos, problem/solution stories). Good content is useful to the reader first, and the product shows up as the natural answer.

## Tools
- `get_product`: the current listing and its claims.
- `inspect_product_files`: the facts sheet, taken from neatlogs' own website. Your only source of truth.
- `mark_claims`: record each claim as true or false against the facts sheet.
- `update_listing`: rewrite the title and description.
- `draft_post`: an X post (waits for human approval; the tracked link is added for you).
- `publish_blog_post`: publish to /blog. Link the product as [neatlogs](/p/neatlogs).

## Rules
- **Accuracy first.** neatlogs is a real company. Before using any claim, inspect the facts sheet and mark it. Never invent features, numbers, prices, customers or quotes, and never speak *for* neatlogs ("we built…"). If something isn't in the facts sheet, leave it out.
- **Write for one reader.** Pick a specific audience and problem (e.g. "your support bot gives a wrong answer and you can't tell why") instead of generic praise.
- **Make it testable.** Lead with a clear headline and one clear call to action, so Analytics can tell whether a headline or angle works.
- Listing: a title that says what it does, then a short description of exactly what the reader gets.
- X posts: honest, specific, under 250 characters.
- Blog posts: 300–800 words, a useful takeaway even for people who never click, then show where neatlogs fits.

## Finish with
One or two sentences: what you changed or published, for whom, and the link.

You are the Support agent for AutoShelf. Great support is how a small team stands out and turns people into advocates.

AutoShelf recommends B2B tools to teams shipping AI agents; right now it sells only **neatlogs**. People who write in are mostly evaluating neatlogs: they want to know if it fits their stack, what the free plan covers, or how to get started.

## Tools
- `list_open_tickets`: open tickets with the customer's message.
- `reply_to_customer`: reply and close the ticket.
- `escalate_to_human`: hand the ticket to the store owner.
- `refund_order`: only for old orders from the retired digital products; neatlogs signups are handled by neatlogs, not us.

## How to answer
- Answer only from what's on the neatlogs listing and facts sheet (free plan, paid plans from $99/month, SDKs for Python, TypeScript and Go, traces, investigations, evals). If you don't know, say so and point them to docs.neatlogs.com, or escalate. Never guess at features or prices.
- Be brief, kind and specific. End with the next step (usually "you can try it free here: /p/neatlogs").
- Account, billing or technical problems inside neatlogs aren't ours to solve: say that neatlogs' own team handles them and escalate so a human can follow up.
- Refunds: you may attempt one for a legacy order; the store rules decide. If it's blocked, escalate. Never retry with a smaller amount to get around the limit.

## Finish with
A one-line summary: tickets answered, escalated, and anything the Operator should know (e.g. "three people asked about Go support").

content.text:
I rewrote all four agents' instruction files in `src/agents/prompts/` using the blog post, and made the code actually load them. They weren't being used before: the real instructions were hardcoded in the `.ts` files, and the `.md` files were stale, mentioning tools that don't exist and digital-goods refunds. Now editing a `.md` and restarting the server changes how that agent behaves.

**Caveat about the blog post:** it's Paras Chopra's 2012 post on the minimal startup team, written about human roles, not AI agents. I used its role definitions, how the roles pair up, and the mistakes it warns about.

**What each agent took from it:**
- **Operator → founder / product manager.** The post says that before product/market fit, the founder works out what the market wants. So its job is to find out what makes the right people want neatlogs and point the specialists at it. It pairs them the way the post does: Analytics finds the leak, Content writes the fix, and Analytics checks the result next run. When there's very little data, it picks actions that teach it something.
- **Analytics → the analytics & marketing expert.** It's "responsible to maximize conversions, in any honest way", and owns the funnel, which sources and posts bring leads, experiments, and cost. It takes on the post's warning against settling for a "good enough" understanding of visitors. It always states how much data a conclusion rests on, and counts leads over visits.
- **Content → the content expert** who "gets" compelling content. It owns the listing, X posts and blog posts. Content should help the reader first, with neatlogs as the natural answer. It writes for one specific reader with a clear headline and one call to action, so the content can be tested, which pairs with Analytics' A/B testing.
- **Support → the post's argument that good support sets a small team apart and wins advocates.** It now handles people evaluating neatlogs before signing up. It answers only from the facts sheet, sends neatlogs' own account and billing problems to a human, and reports patterns to the Operator ("three people asked about Go").

**Rules carried over:** accuracy about neatlogs (claims checked against the facts sheet, nothing invented, never writing as if we built it), the 3-actions limit, the shared token budget, approval before X posts go out, and no getting around refund limits. The files list each agent's real tools, and the Operator is told not to use `set_price`.

**Checked:** the code loads the files, the 16 tests pass, and an offline team run still completes. The offline run uses scripted agents that ignore these instructions, so the real effect only shows on a live run.

Press **Run agent team** on `/ops` to see the new instructions in action. Each run's model calls in neatlogs show the full prompt each agent received.

# API Introduction

> Learn the base URL, headers, authentication, versioning, and response patterns used across the Crustdata API.

Use this page to send your first request and understand the shared conventions across the Company, Person, Job, Web, and Social Post APIs.

## Base URL

All API requests are made to:

```
https://api.crustdata.com
```

## Authentication

Every request must include a Bearer token in the `authorization` header.

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
--header 'authorization: Bearer REDACTED'
```

You can get your API key from the [Crustdata dashboard](https://crustdata.com).

<Warning>
  Keep your API key secret. Do not expose it in client-side code or public
  repositories.
</Warning>

<Note>
  Endpoint availability can vary by plan. Some live Company and Person
  endpoints are enterprise-only. Review [Pricing](/general/pricing) before you
  build a production workflow.
</Note>

## API versioning

Include the `x-api-version` header in every request. The current version is `2025-11-01`.

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
--header 'x-api-version: 2025-11-01'
```

Requests without a version header can default to the latest version, which may introduce breaking changes. Always pin to a specific version.

## Request format

All endpoints accept JSON request bodies with `content-type: application/json`.

```bash theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.crustdata.com/company/identify \
  --header 'authorization: Bearer REDACTED' \
  --header 'content-type: application/json' \
  --header 'x-api-version: 2025-11-01' \
  --data '{"domains": ["retool.com"]}'
```

## Response format

All responses return JSON. Successful requests typically return `200` with the endpoint-specific payload in the response body.

## Error responses

Error responses return JSON with an `error` field and a details field explaining the issue.

<Note>
  Most APIs use `description` for the details field. The Person API uses
  `reason` instead.
</Note>

```json theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "error": "Invalid Request",
    "description": "Exactly one identifier must be provided."
}
```

```json Person API theme={"theme":"vitesse-black"}
{
    "error": "Invalid Request",
    "reason": "Input should be a valid dictionary"
}
```

The Analytics agent can now research neatlogs' competitors with Crustdata. It needs a Crustdata API key before it can actually use it. I tested it against a stand-in that mimics Crustdata's documented responses, not the real API.

**Two new Analytics tools:**
- **`get_competitor_profiles`:** compares neatlogs with its competitors on headcount, 6- and 12-month growth, funding, last funding round, web traffic, and which competitors Crustdata lists for each. By default it covers the six tools neatlogs' own docs name as competitors (it imports traces from them):

  | Competitor | Domain |
  |---|---|
  | Langfuse | langfuse.com |
  | LangSmith | langchain.com |
  | Braintrust | braintrust.dev |
  | Raindrop | raindrop.ai |
  | Arize Phoenix | arize.com |
  | Laminar | lmnr.ai |

- **`find_similar_companies`:** searches for other companies doing AI-agent and LLM observability, to spot competitors we don't know about yet.

**Credits:** a profile costs 2 credits per company, so about 14 for the default seven. Search costs about 0.03 credits per result. Every answer is saved for 7 days, so later runs reuse it for free. Results are trimmed to about 900 tokens, so they fit the run's token budget.

**How the agents use it:**
- **Analytics** does competitor research only when a question needs it, at most once per tool per run. It turns the data into a recommendation like "the big players target X, so aim at teams with Y problem", citing Crustdata.
- **Operator** knows it can ask Analytics for this, and is told to use it when Content needs a sharper angle.
- **Content** may use that angle to pick an audience, but **never names or makes claims about other companies in public posts**. Competitor data stays internal; only facts about neatlogs are checked, so only those go public.

**Checked against the stand-in:** the request format, the trimming, the 7-day cache (the second call didn't touch the network), a company Crustdata can't find (it shows as "not found" instead of crashing), and the clear error when the key is missing. The 16 tests pass and the server is restarted.

**What you need to do:** get a key from app.crustdata.com (there's a free sandbox key for developers), put it in `.env` as `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY=...`, and restart the server. If the sandbox key turns out not to cover the profile endpoint (`/company/enrich`), the agent will show Crustdata's error in the run instead of failing silently.

To see it in action, press **Run agent team**; the Operator decides whether to ask for competitor research. If you want competitor analysis in every run, I can add that to the Operator's instructions.

content.text:
To win this, the demo has to show judges the thing the event is about: agents you'd trust to run unattended. Judges come from neatlogs, Entire and Orchestrator. There's also a hard requirement we don't meet yet.

## Gaps first (these could cost you outright)

| Requirement | Status | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Must use neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai** (25% of score) | neatlogs ✅ · **Entire ❌ not installed, no checkpoints** · **cfo.ai ❌ no business plan** | Install the Entire CLI now so every change from here on gets a checkpoint. Do the cfo.ai plan tomorrow. |
| Public repo | **No remote**, 1 commit, everything since then uncommitted | Create a GitHub repo and commit in logical steps, with Entire attached. |
| A real run | Only offline scripted runs so far | Do 2–3 live runs tonight, so there are real traces and real failures to show. |

## The hook (one sentence for the start of the video)

> **"A startup team of AI agents whose job is to sell neatlogs, and who get debugged by neatlogs when they fail."**

It uses all three sponsors in one loop:
- **neatlogs** traces the team and finds why a run failed.
- A coding agent fixes it, and **Entire** checkpoints that session against the commit.
- The rerun gets compared in neatlogs.
- **cfo.ai** shows the economics: cost per run, cost per lead, runway.
- **Crustdata** powers the competitor research.

## The demo: 5 scenes, about 3 minutes

1. **The goal (0:00–0:20).** "Get teams shipping AI agents to try neatlogs." Press **Run agent team**. Split screen: `/ops` on one side, the neatlogs trace tree filling in live on the other.
2. **Verification (0:20–0:50).** The scenario judges remember. Content finds a false claim on the listing, e.g. "free plan: 1M spans" when the facts sheet says 100k. It refuses to publish it and corrects the listing. Show its thinking in neatlogs. That's the *Verification* focus area, and it shows the agents protect a real brand. The false claim should be planted only in a demo database.
3. **Research → action (0:50–1:30).** Analytics pulls Crustdata profiles of Langfuse, LangSmith and Braintrust and recommends a niche angle. Content publishes a blog post aimed at that niche, live on `/blog`. Click "Try neatlogs", and the lead is credited to that post. That shows *Tool use, Planning and Execution* end to end.
4. **Failure → fix → proof (1:30–2:20).** The scene for the neatlogs and Entire judges. Open a real failed run in neatlogs (an agent running out of budget, a tool error, a wrong product name), use neatlogs' Investigation to get the root cause and fix brief, and hand it to Claude Code. The fix is committed with an **Entire checkpoint** (show the session attached to the commit). Rerun, then compare the two runs in neatlogs: it succeeds with fewer tokens. That's *Recovery and Iteration*, and it uses neatlogs and Entire exactly as the hackathon page describes them.
5. **Unattended and affordable (2:20–3:00).** Run 2 reads what run 1 did and doubles down on the post that brought leads. Show the safety rails: token cap per run, spend cap, claims checked, X posts waiting for approval. End on the cfo.ai sheet: about $0.01 per run, cost per lead, runway.

## What I'd build to make that possible (in order, with ~24h left)

| # | What | Why | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Install Entire, create a public GitHub repo, commit today's work in logical commits | Hard requirement plus scene 4 | ~30 min (you install and log in; I commit) |
| 2 | **Run memory** (`get_past_runs` / `save_note`) | Scene 5: agents improve run over run | ~1h |
| 3 | **Demo database** with one planted false claim, plus a reset script | Scene 2, repeatable for retakes | ~30 min |
| 4 | Live runs with your OpenRouter and Crustdata keys (the hackathon gives everyone 5,000 Crustdata credits) | Real traces, real failures for scene 4 | ~30 min |
| 5 | A **"cost per lead" panel** on `/ops` from the spending log | Ties the agents to the cfo.ai numbers on screen | ~45 min |
| 6 | cfo.ai business plan built from real run costs | Hard requirement plus scene 5 | You sign up; I prepare the numbers |
| 7 (optional) | Deploy on the hackathon EC2 so judges can visit the live store | Impressive, but not required | ~1–2h |

## Building in public (15%, cheap to win)
- Post 3–4 X posts before the deadline: today's journey (3D store → Gumroad style → Bedrock → OpenRouter), a screenshot of the neatlogs trace with thinking, the false-claim catch, and the Entire checkpoint on the fix.
- Submission: quote the official neatlogs post with the repo and video, during 7:00–11:55 PM IST on Monday.

A Shopify pivot can work, but with about 24 hours left it needs to be a deliberate trade, not a restart. Here's my view.

## Why it's tempting
- **Real sales.** A Shopify development store has real products, real checkout and test orders. "The agents made a sale" becomes literally true instead of "a visitor clicked through to neatlogs". That's stronger for "the agent" (30%) and for usefulness (10%), since millions of merchants have this problem.
- **Real tools.** The Shopify Admin API covers everything our agents already do, and more. Products and descriptions map to Content's listing tools, and Shopify's built-in blog maps to `publish_blog_post`. Discount codes, inventory, orders, sales reports and customers are new things the agents could manage.
- **Easier to explain.** "AI team runs a Shopify store while you sleep" is understood in one sentence. "A referral store for neatlogs" needs explaining.

## Why it's risky
- **Time.** Setup takes about 1 hour: a Shopify Partner account, a dev store, a custom app with an Admin API token, and sample products. Rewriting the tools for Shopify's API takes about 4–6 hours. That eats the time we need for the hard requirements.
- **The gaps don't go away.** Entire isn't set up, there's no cfo.ai plan, there's no public repo, and there's been no live run yet. These are 25% of the score whichever store we run.
- **Less original.** "AI agent manages a Shopify store" is a common hackathon idea. "Agents that sell neatlogs and get debugged by neatlogs" is unusually on-theme for these judges.
- **Lost work.** Our own storefront pages, the `/blog` and the lead tracking become mostly unused, because Shopify hosts the store.

## What carries over unchanged
The agent loop, the four roles, token and spend budgets, neatlogs tracing with thinking, the instruction files, Crustdata research, the `/ops` page with "Run agent team", and verifying claims before anything goes public. Only the **tools** change, from our database to Shopify's API. So it's a backend swap, not a restart.

## My recommendation
**Pivot only if you can live with dropping the optional extras.** In order:
1. **Tonight, about 1h:** the hard requirements first. Entire, a public repo, a first live run. These are needed whatever we choose.
2. **Then the swap, 4–6h:** connect a Shopify dev store and move the tools over (products, blog, discounts, orders, sales reports). Keep the same agents and safety rails.
3. **Tomorrow:** cfo.ai plan, demo recording, X posts, submit (7:00–11:55 PM IST).

The demo story stays nearly the same, just more concrete: "the agents run a real Shopify store, catch their own false claims, and get debugged with neatlogs and Entire."

Two questions before I start:
1. **What would the Shopify store sell?** A dev store can generate sample products, or you could pick a niche, like neatHack merch. Having a niche makes the agents' content more interesting.
2. **Why do you want the pivot?** If it's because the neatlogs referral store feels fake (no real sales), Shopify fixes that. If it's something else, there may be a cheaper fix.

## The team's job becomes

> "Here's an empty Shopify store and a budget. Find something worth selling, launch it, and grow sales."

| Agent | What it does in Shopify |
|---|---|
| **Operator** | Sets the plan, picks the niche (with Analytics' evidence), signs off on each launch |
| **Analytics** (+ Crustdata, web research) | Researches the niche and who sells there, then reads Shopify orders and sales reports to judge what's working |
| **Content** | Creates products (title, description, price, tags), writes Shopify blog posts, creates discount codes |
| **Support** | Answers customer messages, flags problems |

- No claim about a product goes public unless it's in its spec sheet.

Install it, then put its **Admin API access token** and store domain (`xxx.myshopify.com`) into `.env`. I'll add the field names to `.env.example`.
2. **Entire CLI** (required by the hackathon): run `! curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`, then sign in. From then on every change I make gets a checkpoint, which we'll show in the demo.
3. **A GitHub repo:** create an empty public repo and send me the URL, or tell me to create it with `gh`. I'll commit today's work in clean steps.

While you do that, I'll build the Shopify connection and tools, test them against a stand-in so they're ready once your token is in, and keep the current store running as a fallback.
