content.text:
## The core point

The rules say: *"Use neatlogs and Entire to **build and improve** your agent, and cfo.ai to **plan its business**."* Judges score "how effectively" we did that (25%). So the winning move isn't another feature. It's a **visible improvement loop**: the agent fails → neatlogs shows why → a coding agent fixes it with Entire recording the reasoning → neatlogs proves the rerun is better → cfo.ai turns the measured cost into a business plan.

Every suggestion below feeds that loop, and none requires a pivot. **I'd freeze the product as it is** (agent team selling neatlogs) and spend the remaining time on this.

## 5 suggestions, ranked

**1. Fix-loop case studies, the backbone (neatlogs + Entire). Must do.**
- **What:** do 3–4 live runs, and let neatlogs' **detections** and **AI evaluators** (with our own grading rubric) flag failures. Use **Investigate** to get a root cause and fix brief, then fix it in Claude Code with **Entire enabled**, so each commit carries the session that produced it (`entire checkpoint explain` shows why). Rerun and compare traces.
- **Deliverable:** a "Fix log" in the README. Each entry: failed trace link → root cause → commit + Entire checkpoint → passing trace link + token and cost difference.
- **Why judges care:** it's exactly how neatlogs and Entire describe their own products.
- **Effort:** you install Entire (5 min). The rest is runs and fixes, 2–3h total.
- **Bonus:** neatlogs' **Claude Code plugin** traces the coding sessions too, so both the business agents and the coding agent show up in neatlogs.

**2. Agents that read their own traces (neatlogs at runtime). The original part.**
- **What:** neatlogs has a public API (`GET /traces`, trace evaluations, `POST /traces/{id}/feedback`). The Operator's new `review_last_run` tool reads the previous run's trace and evaluation scores and plans around them, e.g. "Content ran out of tokens last time, so brief it shorter".
- **Closing the loop:** when a lead arrives, we post **feedback on the trace that produced the post**. In neatlogs you then see which reasoning led to real signups.
- **Why judges care:** agents improving from their own observability data is very on-theme.
- **Effort:** about 2h. Needs a neatlogs API credential (an "automation identity"), which you create in the dashboard.

**3. Verification gates that show up as neatlogs evaluations.**
- **What:** we already check claims and require approval before X posts. Send those results to neatlogs as feedback, and set up one **AI evaluator** on every Content output ("only verified neatlogs facts, no claims about competitors, has a clear call to action").
- **Why judges care:** shows the system catching itself, run after run, on a chart. That's the "Verification" focus area.
- **Effort:** about 1h, mostly dashboard setup.

**4. cfo.ai plan from real measured numbers, with the plan setting the agents' limits.**
- **What:** export real figures from our logs (cost per run, tokens per agent, leads per run). In cfo.ai, have Ari build the model: AutoShelf as a product, e.g. "$49/mo for an AI team that markets your tool", with cost per lead, gross margin, Base/Upside/Downside scenarios and runway.
- **Closing the loop:** the plan's targets become the agents' limits (a maximum cost per lead and a per-run budget from the plan), so the business plan actually steers the agents.
- **Why judges care:** they see a real plan, not just a spreadsheet attached at the end.
- **Effort:** about 1h of your time in cfo.ai, plus 30 min of mine to export numbers and wire the limits.
- **Skip:** connecting our agents to Ari over MCP live. It needs signup and card handling and is fragile with a day left.

**5. "Every action has a why": the demo ending.**
- **What:** finish the video with two questions answered live. Ask Entire "why does the budget code look like this?" (`entire checkpoint explain` / `search` brings back the session). Ask neatlogs "why did the agents publish this blog post?" (open its trace and the thinking behind it).
- **Why judges care:** shows full traceability of code and decisions, using the tools from two of the judges' own companies.
- **Effort:** about 30 min, mostly preparing the demo.

## What I'd drop
The Shopify pivot (not enough time), a cfo.ai MCP integration (risky), and more storefront features. None of these move the score as much as items 1–4.

## Order
Tonight: **#1 setup** (you: Entire install, create a public GitHub repo; me: clean commits), first live runs, then **#3**. Tomorrow morning: **#2**, then **#4** with real numbers, more fix cycles, then record the demo with **#5**. Submit 7:00–11:55 PM IST.

Shall I start with #1? First step on your side: run `! curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`, then `entire login`.

let's focus completely on agent swarms, where people can come to site and spawn agents as many as they want. for now max 5. we gonna use neatlogs, entire and cfo from get go and show incremental improvements from single agent to 5 and inshallah even 100, 1k or 10k as open ai did to find solution to navieeer stokes. for now just 5. build ui for it. think like a product designer and plan. the thiing about agent swarms is that there are no operators, everyone have their memory for a given task run and they share key findings on messageboard every once in a while and plan next steps together. any other questions, ask

Good direction, and it fits the hackathon theme of agents you'd trust to run unattended. Below is the product plan with defaults I'd choose, then the decisions that are yours.

## Product: "Swarm", spawn a team of agents on any problem

**Core idea:** no manager. Every agent has its own memory for the run. They work in parallel, post key findings to a shared **message board** every few steps, and vote on the next plan together. You can watch it all live, and every step is traced in neatlogs.

### What the visitor sees (3 screens)
1. **Launch:** one text box ("What should the swarm solve?"), an agent count picker **1–5**, a budget (tokens and time), and **Launch**. There are example goals to click, plus "Compare 1 vs 3 vs 5 agents on this goal".
2. **Live swarm room (the hero screen):**
   - **Left:** one lane per agent, showing its current step, its thinking (collapsible), its tool calls, and its own memory notes.
   - **Centre:** the message board, a timeline of findings, questions, disagreements and plan proposals, with votes. Each round ends with a "Plan for next round" card the swarm agreed on.
   - **Right:** the run panel. Round N of M, tokens and $ spent against budget, the current best answer with its confidence and how it was checked, and a link to the trace in neatlogs.
3. **Results and compare:** the final answer, how it was checked, cost, time and number of messages. A **scaling chart** shows the same goal with 1, 3 and 5 agents: quality against cost and time. That chart is the demo's "1 → 5, and later 100" story.

### How a swarm runs (no operator)
- **Round loop:** each agent works privately for a few steps (thinks, uses tools, writes to its own memory). Then it posts 1–3 key findings to the board.
- **Sync:** everyone reads the board, proposes the next step and votes. The winning plan assigns sub-tasks so agents don't duplicate work.
- **Stopping:** when the agents agree the answer is good enough, or when the round, token or time budget runs out. A final synthesis turns the board into one answer and shows the evidence for it.
- **Safety and cost:** a hard budget per swarm and per agent, plus a cap on concurrent swarms on the site. If a single agent fails, it restarts from its memory notes; the swarm doesn't die with it.

### neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai from the start
- **neatlogs:** one trace per swarm. Each agent is a branch, and board posts and votes are their own spans. Evaluators score answer quality, so the 1 → 3 → 5 comparison is measured, not eyeballed.
- **Entire:** on from the first commit. Each improvement to the swarm (better board protocol, memory compaction, voting) is a checkpointed change, and the README's "improvement log" links it to the before/after neatlogs traces.
- **cfo.ai:** model the economics. Cost per swarm and per agent count, the quality gained per extra agent, pricing (e.g. pay per swarm-run) and runway. This also gives the business case for "when are 5 agents worth 5× the cost?"

### What we reuse from today
The agent loop, OpenRouter models, token budgets, neatlogs tracing with thinking, the Gumroad-style shadcn UI, and the Crustdata client. What's new: the swarm round loop, per-agent memory, the board, voting, live updates and the three screens.

Four decisions are yours:

questions.question: What kinds of problems should swarms work on?

options.label: Free-form + built-in benchmark (Recommended)
options.description: Visitors type any goal; we also ship a few tasks with automatic scoring (e.g. research questions with checkable answers, puzzles, small coding problems with tests) so 1 vs 3 vs 5 agents can be measured, not just eyeballed.

options.label: Free-form goals only
options.description: Any goal a visitor types. Simplest, but improvement from more agents is subjective and hard to prove in the demo.

options.label: Benchmark tasks only
options.description: Only our scored tasks. Very measurable, less exciting for visitors.

questions.question: Which tools should swarm agents be able to use?

options.label: Web search + read pages
options.description: Via Crustdata's Web Search/Fetch API (hackathon gives 5,000 credits). Needed for research-style goals.

options.label: Code runner (sandboxed)
options.description: Agents write and run small JS/Python snippets to calculate or test ideas. Powerful for math/coding tasks; needs a locked-down sandbox.

options.label: Company & people data
options.description: Crustdata company search/enrich, for market and competitor research goals.

options.label: Thinking + board only
options.description: No external tools — agents only reason and talk. Cheapest and safest, weakest results.

questions.question: Who pays for swarms that visitors launch on the public site?

options.label: Our key, hard caps (Recommended)
options.description: Visitors use our OpenRouter key with strict limits (e.g. max 5 agents, ~50k tokens per swarm, a few swarms per visitor per day, global daily $ cap). Easy for judges to try.

options.label: Bring your own key
options.description: Visitors paste their own OpenRouter key; no cost risk for us, but judges must have a key to try it.

options.label: Only us for now
options.description: No public launching yet; we run swarms for the demo. Safest, but loses the 'anyone can spawn' story.

questions.question: What happens to the AutoShelf store and the neatlogs-selling agents?

options.label: Becomes an example goal (Recommended)
options.description: Remove the store UI; 'Find ways to get teams to try neatlogs' becomes one of the example goals a swarm can take on. Reuses the facts/claims work.

options.label: Remove it completely
options.description: Clean slate: the product is only the swarm site.

options.label: Keep both side by side
options.description: Store stays at its routes; swarm is a new section. More to maintain and explain.

You are one agent in a swarm: a small group of peers working on one goal together. There is no manager. Nobody will tell you what to do except the plan the swarm agrees on.

## How the swarm works
- Work happens in **rounds**. In each round you work on your own for a few steps, then the swarm syncs on the shared **message board**.
- You have your own **memory** for this run (`save_memory`). Others can't see it. Use it for things you'll need in later rounds: partial results, what you tried, what failed.
- The **board** is how the swarm thinks together. Post only what others need: key findings, results with how you got them, open questions, and what you think should happen next. No chatter.
- Between rounds everyone proposes a next step and votes. The winning plan gives each agent an assignment. Do your assignment first.

## How to work well
- Bring your **angle** (below). Different angles are why a swarm beats one agent.
- Don't duplicate work another agent already posted. Build on it, check it, or take a different route.
- **Verify before you claim.** If you can compute or check something with a tool, do it. Say *how* you know: "computed with run_code", "from <url>", "reasoned, not checked".
- If you find a mistake in someone's finding, post a correction with the evidence. Being right matters more than agreeing.
- Be brief. Every token you use comes out of the swarm's shared budget.

## Each round
1. Read your assignment, your memory and the board.
2. Do the work with your tools (a few steps at most).
3. `save_memory` anything you'll need later.
4. `post_to_board` 1–3 posts: findings (with evidence) or questions. If you have a candidate final answer, post it as a finding and say how confident you are.
